Ganglioside_Antibodies.clinical_significance: IgG antibodies to GQ1b are found in most patients with Miller Fisher syndrome and its incomplete forms; a positive result does not establish the diagnosis on its own. Clinical correlation recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Polyradiculoneuropathy pattern (demyelinating or axonal features, absent F-waves, sural sparing where present); may be normal in the first week; no decrement on repetitive stimulation
action_criteria.label: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG with repetitive nerve stimulation
action_criteria.rationale: Nerve conduction studies show the peripheral nerve involvement behind the areflexia, and repetitive stimulation tests the neuromuscular junction, the main alternative for bilateral ptosis [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Albuminocytological dissociation: raised protein with cells <5/mm3 (5-50/mm3 compatible but prompts an alternative; >50/mm3 suggests another diagnosis); protein may be normal in the first week
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein and glucose
action_criteria.rationale: CSF albuminocytological dissociation supports a GBS-spectrum disorder; normal cells exclude an infective or malignant cause [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Anti-GQ1b IgG positive (1:320), anti-GT1a negative: places the ptosis with areflexia in the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome
action_criteria.label: Serum anti-GQ1b IgG: acute bilateral ptosis with areflexia is an incomplete Miller Fisher form only with the antibody
action_criteria.rationale: Isolated acute ptosis is an incomplete form of Miller Fisher syndrome (Wakerley 2014) that the clinical picture alone cannot establish; EAN/PNS 2023 advises anti-GQ1b when the MFS spectrum is suspected, and here the result carries the diagnosis against ocular myasthenia.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies negative
action_criteria.label: Acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies to exclude ocular myasthenia gravis
action_criteria.rationale: Bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoplegia is the presentation of ocular myasthenia gravis, the mimic that must be excluded.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No midbrain or other brainstem lesion; no cranial nerve enhancement
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with gadolinium to exclude a midbrain lesion
action_criteria.rationale: Bilateral ptosis can arise from a lesion of the central caudal oculomotor nucleus; a normal MRI removes it.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No improvement in ptosis after ice
action_criteria.label: Optional bedside ice pack test for myasthenic ptosis
action_criteria.rationale: A cheap bedside test for myasthenic ptosis; the antibodies and neurophysiology already answer the question.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Baseline values before treatment; abnormal liver tests or low albumin mark a higher risk of a severe course; no metabolic or toxic alternative
action_criteria.label: Baseline blood tests: full blood count, renal function and electrolytes, liver tests, albumin, glucose and CK
action_criteria.rationale: Routine blood tests exclude metabolic causes and give a baseline [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC in L, % predicted and mL/kg, MIP and MEP, with the trend; ICU-level monitoring if FVC <20 mL/kg or <60% predicted, MIP weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O, a fall of more than 30%, or bulbar weakness with weak cough
action_criteria.label: Bedside respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP), repeated serially while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Anti-GQ1b disease can extend to bulbar, limb and respiratory weakness; a baseline and serial measurements detect it [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous telemetry with blood pressure monitoring: normal sinus rhythm 72-96 bpm and blood pressure 108/66 to 126/80 mmHg in the first 24 hours; autonomic instability (rate and blood pressure lability, bradyarrhythmia) requires continued monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.label: Continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while weakness progresses
action_criteria.rationale: Autonomic dysfunction is common in GBS and can cause bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability; monitoring continues while weakness progresses [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm 84 bpm with normal intervals (QTc 418 ms) and no conduction or ST-T abnormality: a baseline while autonomic involvement can still develop
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline 12-lead ECG screens for autonomic dysrhythmia and conduction abnormality and gives the QTc before treatment [EAN_PNS_2023].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No current medications, so nothing to review
action_criteria.label: Optional interaction check (no current medications)
action_criteria.rationale: She takes no medicines and no drug treatment is planned, so the check cannot change management (ROUND_POLICY ruling 6).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on immunotherapy in Miller Fisher syndrome; not needed for the diagnosis or the management decision
action_criteria.label: Optional literature search on treatment of Miller Fisher syndrome and its incomplete forms
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].

Do not start pyridostigmine or treat for myasthenia gravis: areflexia, normal repetitive stimulation and single-fibre EMG, negative AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies and a positive anti-GQ1b argue against it.
required_recommendations: Admit for monitoring without IVIg or plasma exchange while deficits stay restricted to ptosis and areflexia: immunotherapy is not routinely advised in Miller Fisher-spectrum disease [Leonhard_2019, Wakerley_2014].

Monitor for ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, bulbar, limb or respiratory involvement or reduced consciousness (overlap with GBS or Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis), with serial FVC, MIP and MEP and swallow checks; treat with IVIg or plasma exchange if limb weakness, bulbar or respiratory involvement develops [EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring while deficits may still progress.
Explain that anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome usually recovers over weeks to months, and arrange neurology follow-up with mobility support while she cannot open her eyes.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.

accepted: Anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome (acute bilateral ptosis with areflexia), Guillain-Barré syndrome spectrum

differential.key_features: Bilateral ptosis is the cardinal ocular MG sign, but there is no fatigability or diurnal variation, reflexes are absent, repetitive stimulation and single-fibre EMG are normal, the ice pack test is negative where done, and AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies are negative.

differential.diagnosis: Progression to complete Miller Fisher syndrome or GBS overlap
differential.key_features: The triad is not met (no ophthalmoplegia or ataxia) but she lies within the same anti-GQ1b spectrum; monitoring during admission detects progression.
Ptosis can be an early sign, but pupils and eye movements are normal, there is no descending weakness, repetitive stimulation is normal and there is no food or wound exposure.
Proximal limb weakness and autonomic features dominate, CMAPs are low with an incremental response; here strength and CMAPs are normal and repetitive stimulation shows no abnormality.
Chronic course over years, not 7 days; does not cause areflexia.
Bilateral isolated ptosis without other brainstem findings is rare in stroke, and the brain MRI is normal.

key_clinical_evidence: Global areflexia in a patient with isolated ptosis is the discriminating sign: myasthenia gravis preserves reflexes.

Acute bilateral ptosis with areflexia and anti-GQ1b IgG is an incomplete form of Miller Fisher syndrome within the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome [Wakerley_2014]; the antibody supports but does not establish the diagnosis on its own.
CSF protein 62 mg/dL with 3 cells/mm3 and absent F-waves and H-reflexes with mild demyelinating features support a GBS-spectrum disorder.
IVIg and plasma exchange are not routinely advised in Miller Fisher-spectrum disease; the scored behaviour is admission and monitoring for overlap [Leonhard_2019].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Global areflexia, CSF albuminocytological dissociation, absent late responses, normal neuromuscular transmission tests, negative myasthenia antibodies and a positive anti-GQ1b IgG place the ptosis in the anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome, not myasthenia gravis.
red_herrings.data_point: Isolated bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoplegia or weakness
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on myasthenia gravis as the textbook bilateral-ptosis aetiology.

general.query: treatment of Miller Fisher syndrome and its incomplete forms

results.finding: In Miller Fisher syndrome, IVIg and plasma exchange are not routinely advised because most patients recover fully without treatment; patients are monitored for overlap with GBS or Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis, which may need treatment.

general.summary: IVIg and plasma exchange are not routinely advised in Miller Fisher syndrome; monitoring for overlap with GBS or Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis is advised [Leonhard_2019].

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL study. 1. Mildly prolonged distal motor latencies and borderline conduction velocities in bilateral median motor nerves; CMAP amplitudes preserved. 2. Mildly reduced sural sensory amplitudes bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves (median and peroneal) and H-reflexes bilaterally. 4. No decrement on 3 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation. 5. Normal jitter on single-fibre EMG. Mild demyelinating features with absent late responses; no evidence of a neuromuscular junction disorder.

quantitative_data.pattern: Mild demyelinating features with absent F-waves and H-reflexes; normal neuromuscular transmission

metadata.difficulty_description: Isolated bilateral ptosis with areflexia in the anti-GQ1b antibody spectrum: closely mimics myasthenia gravis; areflexia and the anti-GQ1b antibody are the discriminating findings
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions (NCS/EMG with RNS, CSF, baseline labs, respiratory function, telemetry), 2 recommended mimic exclusions (myasthenia antibodies, brain MRI), 1 red herring (bilateral ptosis).
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 GBS audit: spine MRI is optional and limited to five cases with a concrete cord, traumatic, postoperative or infiltrative alternative; generic hidden MRI reports removed.

patient.chief_complaint: Seven-day progressive bilateral ptosis with complete inability to open eyes, preserved eye movements, no limb weakness, global areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. K. is a 33-year-old teacher presenting with a 7-day history of progressive bilateral ptosis. The ptosis began in the left eye and spread to involve the right eye 5 days later. She now has nearly complete bilateral ptosis and cannot open her eyelids voluntarily without using her fingers. She reports mild generalized malaise and fatigue with routine activities over the same period. She denies diplopia. She has no difficulty swallowing, speaking, or breathing. She notes no weakness in her arms or legs and was able to walk to the emergency department without difficulty. She has no sensory symptoms. Her ptosis does not vary through the day and does not worsen with prolonged activity. There is no prior history of similar symptoms. She recalls no recent respiratory illness, gastrointestinal illness, or other viral syndrome preceding the onset. She denies exposure to spoiled food, wounds, or ticks. She takes no medications.

neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin intact. No ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis: unable to open the eyelids voluntarily without assistance; minimal lid elevation on attempted upgaze. No fatigability on sustained upgaze. Pupils equal, round, reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements full in all directions; no ophthalmoplegia. No diplopia. Bell's phenomenon preserved. No facial weakness. No dysarthria. Gag preserved.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Normal bulk and tone throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Global areflexia: absent biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar and Achilles reflexes bilaterally. Plantars downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, proprioception in all extremities.
